original.target_description: Original source contains multiple candidate tests of conditional-stimulus valence in Experiments 1 and 2; assigned test remains ambiguous.

n.sample_role: Candidate recruitment counts: undergraduate participants, not verified critical-model analytic N.
n.exclusions: Experiment 1: evaluation data lost for three participants; other losses measure-specific. Experiment 2: measure-specific recording losses; valence analytic N not explicitly established for the unresolved target.
n.quote:
Participants. Thirty-six (21 female) undergraduate students aged 17-52 years (M =

21.71) provided informed consent and volunteered participation in exchange for course credit.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of two groups (instruction/removal, control). The

pre-experimental ratings data of one participant was lost due to a recording error and evaluation

data of three participants and the electrodermal responses of one participant were lost due

problems with the recording device. These participants were included in the analyses of all

remaining measures. ... Participants. Forty-four (26 female) undergraduate students volunteered participation in

exchange for course credit. The participants’ ages ranged from 16-59 (M = 22.77). All

participants consented to the experiment and were fully informed. Participants were randomly

assigned to one of two groups (instruction/removal, control). Recording error resulted in the loss

of two participants’ pre-experimental ratings data, four participants’ post-experimental ratings

data, and one participants’ fear potentiated startle data. These participants were included in the ... analyses of all remaining measures.

es.location: Canonical manuscript form-feed pages 18–20 and 25–27 (valence results); journal p. 23 is not mapped in this manuscript.
es.quote:
Multivariate F values (Phillai’s Trace) and partial eta-squares are reported for all main

effects and interactions. ... During extinction, both groups gave lower pleasantness ratings to the CS+ (M = -0.82,

SD = 0.81) in comparison with the CS- (M = -0.12, SD = 0.87), and both conditional stimuli were

rated as more pleasant as extinction progressed. The analyses confirmed these impressions

revealing main effects of CS, F(1, 31) = 15.79, p  .001, ηp2 = .337, and block, F(3, 29) = 5.49, p

= .004, ηp2 = .362. ... As the influence of the instructional manipulation was expected in early extinction, the

analyses were run excluding blocks three and four. This did not change the pattern of results,

with analyses revealing a main effect of CS, F(1, 31) = 18.36, p  .001, ηp2 = .372, and a main

effect of block, F(1, 31) = 11.05, p = .002, ηp2 = .263. All remaining main effects and

interactions did not attain significance, largest (block × group, F(1, 31) = 1.66, p = .207, ηp2 =

.051. ... However, the CS × block × group interaction was not significant, F(1,

42) = 0.07, p = .797, ηp2 = .002, confirming that the instructional manipulation did not

differentially affect the conditional stimulus valence evaluations.

replication.target_description: Unassigned side; not examined in this source-grouped task.

notes: Identity: source header title matches the assigned original reference; title page identifies Camilla C. Luck and Ottmar V. Lipp. Full primary research manuscript with methods, results, references, figures and appendix, rather than an abstract or secondary report. Title-page subtitle uses Physiological Responses; header uses physiological responding. The assigned DOI/year/journal metadata are not printed in this manuscript and were not independently verified; no network used. No PDF supplied, so no PDF rendering or journal-page alignment was possible. The locator gives no original experiment identifier or specific valence test/phase. Both Experiments 1 and 2 measure conditional-stimulus valence during full extinction, early extinction and post-experimental ratings. Manuscript pages cannot be securely mapped to journal p. 23. Even within Experiment 1 the description does not distinguish persistent CS valence from the effect of instruction on valence. Selecting one printed test would invent target correspondence. Printed candidates (not assigned estimates): Experiment 1 full-extinction CS main effect F(1, 31) = 15.79, p < .001, partial eta-squared .337; block effect F(3, 29) = 5.49, p = .004, partial eta-squared .362; early-extinction CS main effect F(1, 31) = 18.36, p < .001, partial eta-squared .372; early block × group F(1, 31) = 1.66, p = .207, partial eta-squared .051; final-block CS main effect F(1, 31) = 7.78, p = .009, partial eta-squared .201. Experiment 2 full-extinction CS main effect F(1, 41) = 6.58, p = .014, partial eta-squared .138; early-extinction CS × block × group F(1, 42) = 0.07, p = .797, partial eta-squared .002. Each p above is retained with its own printed test. Experiment 1 recruited 36 with evaluation data lost for three; Experiment 2 recruited 44 with measure-specific missingness and whole-sample/restricted analyses described. Recruitment counts are not assigned analytic N. No N derived from df, subtraction, or undocumented final groups. Unassigned replication and reported_success are placeholders only.
